name: Apple Scab
description: Apple scab is one of the most serious and economically destructive fungal diseases of apple and crabapple trees worldwide. It is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis and can result in crop losses of up to 70% by reducing fruit quality, causing deformation, and triggering premature leaf and fruit drop.
symptoms: Superficial, velvety dark-olive-to-black spots on leaves and fruits
Spots become scab-like and corky with age
Lesions with feathery, indistinct margins on leaves
Young leaves become curled and distorted during severe infection
Premature leaf and fruit drop
Fruit becomes misshapen and may crack
Fruit lesions become corky, cracked, and rough
causes: Fungus Venturia inaequalis
Primary spores (ascospores) released from fungal bodies in fallen infected leaves during spring rains
Secondary spores (conidia) produced on lesions spread disease further
Prolonged moisture and cool spring temperatures favor infection
Fungus overwinters in dead infected leaves on the ground
treatments: Apply protectant fungicides starting at green tip (first susceptible tissue emergence)
Use captan, mancozeb, or myclobutanil-based fungicides
Apply throughout the season, especially during wet periods
Remove and destroy infected fallen leaves to reduce inoculum
Prune canopy to improve air circulation and reduce moisture
prevention: Plant disease-resistant apple varieties
Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn
Prune trees to open the canopy and improve air drying
Apply preventive fungicide sprays before disease onset in spring
Avoid overhead irrigation that wets leaves
Irrigate in early morning so leaves can dry during the day

name: Apple Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot)
description: Black rot is a widespread and damaging fungal disease of apple and crabapple trees caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It causes fruit rot, leaf spots (frogeye leaf spot), and branch cankers. The fruit rot phase can render fruit unmarketable, while cankers weaken and kill branches.
symptoms: Leaf spots start as small purple spots that enlarge with brownish-tan centers and purple outlines (frog-eye appearance)
Heavily infected leaves drop prematurely
Fruit lesions begin at calyx end as brown/rotted areas
Fruit lesions develop concentric rings resembling a bull's-eye
Complete fruit mummification or black rot on fruit
Reddish-brown, sunken, rough-barked cankers on limbs and trunks
Diseased limbs may be fully girdled by cankers and die back
causes: Fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa (synonym: Diplodia seriata)
Fungus overwinters in cankers, mummified fruit, and dead plant tissue
Spores released during wet periods and spread by rain, wind, and insects
Wounds from winter injury, fire blight, or pruning serve as entry points
Warm, wet weather conditions favor spore dispersal and infection
treatments: Remove and destroy mummified fruits, dead limbs, and infected plant material
Prune out cankers at least 15 cm (6 inches) beyond visible infection
Apply copper-based fungicides or captan as needed for fruit rot control
Use EBDC fungicides (Mancozeb, Polyram) in commercial settings
Apply lime-sulfur or Daconil-based products for homeowners
prevention: Maintain good sanitation by removing fallen debris and mummified fruit
Prune and destroy infected branches during dormancy
Reduce tree stress through proper watering and fertilization
Manage fire blight, as infected wood increases susceptibility
Apply preventive fungicide programs early in the season
Remove any injured or insect-damaged fruits promptly

name: Cedar Apple Rust
description: Cedar apple rust is a fungal disease caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae that requires both apple/crabapple trees and juniper/cedar trees to complete its two-year life cycle. It cannot spread directly between apple trees. Repeated infections can weaken trees and reduce fruit production.
symptoms: Pale yellow to orange pinhead-sized spots on upper leaf surface in early spring
Spots enlarge to bright yellow/orange lesions over time
Small bulges develop on the undersides of infected leaves in midsummer
Hairlike cylindrical tubes (hyphae) emerge from undersurface lesions
Leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely
Galls on juniper/cedar trees swell and produce orange gelatinous spore horns in spring
Fruit and young twigs may also be infected
causes: Fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae
Requires two host plants: apple/crabapple and Eastern red cedar/juniper
Spores from cedar galls blown by wind to apple trees during rainy spring weather
Spores produced on apple/crabapple only infect junipers the following year
Cool, wet spring conditions favor infection
treatments: Apply protective fungicides (myclobutanil, copper, sulfur) starting at bud break
Spray weekly during bloom period when junipers are releasing spores
Treat junipers with copper solution (4 applications between late August and October)
Remove heavily infected leaves and branches
Use SERENADE (Bacillus subtilis) for organic control
prevention: Avoid planting Eastern red cedar/juniper within several hundred yards of apple trees
Plant disease-resistant apple and crabapple varieties
Remove nearby cedar/juniper trees if possible
Apply dormant oil spray in late winter before bud break
Apply fungicides preventively before leaf spots appear
Ensure proper tree spacing for good air circulation

name: Healthy
description: The apple plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage. Leaves are green, fruit is developing normally, and the plant shows vigorous growth.
symptoms: Leaves are deep green, firm, and free of spots or lesions
Fruit develops normally with good size, color, and shape
Bark is smooth and free of cankers or sunken areas
New shoots show vigorous, upright growth
No premature leaf or fruit drop
Roots are firm and white with no signs of rot
causes: Adequate soil nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium)
Proper irrigation without waterlogging or drought stress
Well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-7.0)
Good air circulation from proper pruning
Absence of pest or pathogen pressure
Appropriate sunlight exposure (full sun, 6-8 hours daily)
treatments: Continue regular pruning to maintain open canopy and air circulation
Apply balanced fertilizer based on soil test results
Maintain consistent irrigation schedule
Monitor regularly for early signs of disease or pest activity
Apply preventive fungicide sprays during high-risk periods (wet spring weather)
prevention: Maintain regular pruning to promote air circulation
Apply balanced fertilizer as needed
Monitor regularly for early signs of disease or pests
Practice good orchard sanitation
Ensure adequate irrigation without over-watering

name: Healthy
description: The blueberry plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage.
symptoms: Leaves are dark green, glossy, and free of spots or discoloration
Berries develop full size with normal blue color at ripeness
Stems and canes are firm and free of lesions
Strong new shoot growth each season
No unusual leaf drop or wilting
Root system is healthy and white when examined
causes: Proper soil pH maintained between 4.5 and 5.5
Consistent moisture with well-drained soil
Adequate organic matter in soil
Full sun exposure (6-8 hours daily)
Absence of pest or pathogen pressure
Balanced nutrient availability, especially iron and manganese at low pH
treatments: Test and adjust soil pH annually using sulfur or acidifying fertilizers
Apply acidifying fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) as needed
Maintain 2-4 inch mulch layer to retain moisture and suppress weeds
Prune out old, unproductive canes every 1-2 years
Monitor for early signs of disease such as mummy berry or botrytis
prevention: Maintain proper soil pH (4.5–5.5) for optimal plant health
Ensure well-drained soil and consistent moisture
Prune regularly to improve air circulation
Monitor for early signs of disease or pests
Avoid overhead irrigation to minimize leaf wetness

name: Cherry Powdery Mildew
description: Powdery mildew of cherry is caused by the obligate biotrophic fungus Podosphaera clandestina. Mid- and late-season sweet cherry cultivars are commonly affected. The disease covers cherry surfaces with white fungal growth, rendering fruit unmarketable. Season-long disease control of both leaves and fruit is critical.
symptoms: Light, roughly-circular, powdery white patches on young, susceptible leaves
White cotton-like growth on affected leaf areas
Severe leaf infection causes curling and blistering
Small black fungal bodies (cleistothecia) visible in colonies toward end of season
Infected fruit develops circular, slightly sunken lesions
Deformed fruit when infected young
Premature defoliation in severe cases
causes: Fungus Podosphaera clandestina
Obligate biotrophic fungus requiring living host tissue
Spreads via airborne spores to new susceptible tissue
Warm, dry conditions with low humidity favor spore germination
Young, actively growing leaves are most susceptible
Older leaves develop natural (ontogenic) resistance
treatments: Apply fungicides (myclobutanil, sulfur, or demethylation inhibitors) starting at petal fall
Continue applications through pit hardening
Many fungicides used for brown rot control are also effective against powdery mildew
Remove and destroy infected leaves and debris
Improve air circulation around the tree
prevention: Plant resistant cherry cultivars (e.g., Chelan, Lambert, Regina)
Prune trees regularly to improve airflow and reduce dense canopy
Apply protectant fungicides before symptoms appear (best applied at first cover timing)
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes succulent growth
Monitor regularly from petal fall through the growing season

name: Healthy
description: The cherry plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage.
symptoms: Leaves are dark green, firm, and free of spots or lesions
Fruit develops with normal size, color, and firmness
Bark and branches are smooth, free of cankers or gummosis
Vigorous shoot growth during the growing season
No premature leaf drop or wilting
Flowers bloom normally and fruit sets well
causes: Well-drained, loamy soil with pH 6.0-7.0
Adequate irrigation, especially during fruit development
Full sun exposure (6-8 hours daily)
Proper pruning for open canopy and air circulation
Absence of pest or pathogen pressure
Balanced fertilization with adequate potassium and calcium
treatments: Prune annually after harvest to maintain open, well-ventilated canopy
Apply balanced fertilizer based on soil and leaf tissue test results
Maintain consistent irrigation during fruit development stage
Monitor for powdery mildew, brown rot, and bacterial spot throughout season
Apply preventive fungicide program during bloom and early fruit development
prevention: Prune annually to maintain open canopy and air circulation
Water at soil level to avoid wetting foliage
Monitor regularly for early signs of disease
Practice good orchard sanitation, removing debris and fallen fruit

name: Corn Gray Leaf Spot (Cercospora Leaf Spot)
description: Gray leaf spot, caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis, is considered one of the most significant yield-limiting diseases of corn worldwide. It is most severe in areas with minimum tillage and corn-on-corn rotations. Extended periods of high humidity and warm temperatures favor disease development.
symptoms: Small, tan to gray rectangular lesions on leaves (up to 2 inches long and 1/4 inch wide)
Lesions run parallel to leaf veins, delimited by vein margins
Lesions start as small necrotic spots with chlorotic (yellow) halos
Lesions develop a gray coloration as sporulation begins
Multiple lesions coalesce and form large necrotic areas
Entire leaves may be killed (blighted) under severe conditions
Symptoms first appear on lower leaves 2-3 weeks before tasseling
causes: Fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis
Fungus survives in corn crop residue on the soil surface
Spores dispersed by wind and splashing rain onto corn leaves
Prolonged periods of high humidity (>95%) and warm temperatures (64-81°F) favor infection
No-till or minimum-till farming increases disease risk due to more crop residue
Corn-on-corn rotation significantly increases disease pressure
treatments: Apply foliar fungicides containing pyraclostrobin, strobilurin, azoxystrobin + propiconazole, or prothioconazole + trifloxystrobin
Treatment most effective when applied early, before disease spreads above ear leaf
Weigh fungicide cost against potential yield loss and disease severity
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids
Practice crop rotation (avoid corn-on-corn)
Use tillage to bury crop residue and reduce inoculum
Monitor fields regularly and scout lower leaves for early symptoms
Avoid poorly drained soils or fields prone to extended dew periods

name: Corn Common Rust
description: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi and occurs every growing season in corn. It is most problematic during prolonged periods of cool, wet weather. While it rarely causes significant yield loss in commercial hybrids, severe infections can lead to leaf chlorosis and death.
symptoms: Rust-colored to dark brown, elongated pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules contain cinnamon-brown urediniospores
Pustules darken as they age
Leaves and sheaths can be infected
Under severe conditions, leaf chlorosis (yellowing) and death may occur
Pustules appear sporadically, typically between V12 and R4 growth stages
causes: Fungus Puccinia sorghi
Spores are windborne and travel long distances from southern overwintering areas
Cool temperatures and wet conditions favor disease development
No soil survival - the fungus does not overwinter in northern states
treatments: Apply fungicides when few pustules appear on leaves before tasseling
Fungicide applications are most beneficial on susceptible hybrids during cool, wet seasons
Triazole and strobilurin fungicides are effective
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids (most commercial hybrids have good resistance)
Scout fields regularly for early signs of rust pustules
Timely planting to avoid peak infection periods

name: Corn Northern Leaf Blight (NCLB)
description: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum and has become an increasingly troublesome disease in the United States. Severe outbreaks can cause 30-50% yield loss in dent corn when established before tasseling. The disease also causes significant quality reduction in sweet and silage corn.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped (elliptical) tan to grayish-green lesions on leaves (1 to 6 inches long)
Early symptoms are small, water-soaked lesions with gray-green margins
Mature lesions are tan/gray and run parallel to leaf veins
Lesions produce olive-green or black fungal spores in humid conditions
Symptoms first appear on lower leaves and spread upward
Leaf blades, sheaths, and ear husks may show symptoms on susceptible hybrids
Lesions coalesce causing large areas of blighted leaf tissue
causes: Fungus Exserohilum turcicum
Fungus overwinters in corn crop residue
Spores are wind and rain dispersed to new corn crops
Moderate temperatures (64-81°F) and prolonged leaf wetness (6-18 hours) favor infection
Frequent rainfall, high humidity, and heavy dew increase disease severity
No-till fields with continuous corn are at highest risk
treatments: Apply foliar fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins, or combinations) when disease is present on lower leaves before tasseling
Most effective if 50% or more plants show disease on or above the ear leaf
Residue management can reduce inoculum in future seasons
prevention: Plant hybrids with resistance genes (Ht1, Ht2, Ht3, or HtN)
Practice crop rotation to reduce corn residue inoculum
Use tillage to bury infected residue
Scout fields regularly during the growing season
Monitor local weather conditions for periods of extended humidity

name: Healthy
description: The corn plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage.
symptoms: Leaves are deep green and upright with no lesions or spots
Stalks are firm and erect with no soft or hollow areas
Ears fill out completely with uniform kernel development
Root system is extensive and firm
Tassels and silks develop normally and pollination is complete
No signs of premature firing (leaf death) on lower leaves
causes: Adequate soil nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium levels
Optimal soil pH between 6.0 and 7.0
Consistent moisture with good soil drainage
Adequate plant population and row spacing for air circulation
Absence of foliar fungal, bacterial, or viral pressure
Warm growing temperatures (60-95°F)
treatments: Apply side-dress nitrogen fertilizer at V6 stage if needed
Maintain consistent irrigation especially during silking and grain fill
Scout fields weekly for early signs of disease or pest pressure
Apply foliar fungicide preventively on susceptible hybrids in high-risk environments
prevention: Practice crop rotation to avoid buildup of soil-borne pathogens
Use certified disease-free seed
Apply seed fungicide treatments
Monitor fields regularly for early disease signs
Maintain proper plant spacing for adequate air circulation

name: Grape Black Rot
description: Grape black rot is a serious fungal disease caused by Guignardia bidwellii that primarily affects immature berries, young canes, and leaves. It is most destructive during warm, wet seasons and can cause near-complete fruit loss if left unmanaged. It is mainly a disease of immature plant parts.
symptoms: Small, circular, concentric spots (grayish-brown with black margins) on leaves
Black, shriveled, mummified berries (raisins) remaining on vine
Dark lesions starting on immature berries
Lesions expand, turning berries brown then completely black
Reddish-brown elongated cankers on young shoots and stems
Small, dark fruiting bodies (pycnidia) embedded in lesions
causes: Fungus Guignardia bidwellii
Fungus overwinters in mummified berries and infected canes left in the vineyard
Spores released during warm, wet weather in spring
Warm and wet weather (70-90°F) during spring and summer favors infection
Most infections occur on immature plant tissue
treatments: Apply protectant fungicides (captan, mancozeb, myclobutanil, or copper) starting at bud break
Continue applications through 4-5 weeks after bloom
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit and infected canes
Prune vines to improve air circulation
prevention: Practice thorough sanitation: remove mummified berries and prune out infected canes each season
Cultivate soil to bury diseased vineyard debris
Protect pruning wounds from fungal infection
Apply preventive fungicide sprays starting before bloom
Select more resistant grape varieties where possible

name: Grape Esca (Black Measles)
description: Esca (Black Measles) is a complex grapevine trunk disease caused by wood-infecting fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium minimum. It is considered a disease of older vines (5+ years) and is one of the most devastating threats to viticulture worldwide. There is currently no effective curative treatment.
symptoms: Interveinal 'tiger stripe' patterns on leaves (dark red in red cultivars, yellow/chlorotic in white cultivars)
Leaf stripes dry out and become necrotic
Leaves may dry completely and drop prematurely
Small, round, dark berry spots bordered by brown-purple rings
In severe cases, berries crack, dry, or rot
Dark brown/black vascular streaking visible in cross-section of trunk
Apoplectic form: sudden wilting and death of entire shoots or vine within a season
causes: Complex of wood-infecting fungi: Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, and various basidiomycetes (Fomitiporia mediterranea)
Pathogens enter through pruning wounds
Infected propagation material can introduce the disease to new vineyards
Disease more common in vines 10+ years old
No known resistant grapevine varieties
treatments: No effective curative chemical treatment currently available
Remove and destroy heavily infected vines
Surgical removal of infected wood where possible
Biological control with Trichoderma species applied prophylactically to pruning wounds
prevention: Protect fresh pruning wounds immediately with fungicidal wound sealants or Trichoderma-based products
Use clean, certified disease-free planting material from reputable nurseries
Prune during dry weather to minimize infection risk
Remove and destroy infected plant material from the vineyard
Replant with young vines in chronically affected areas

name: Grape Leaf Blight (Isariopsis Leaf Spot)
description: Grape leaf blight, also known as Isariopsis leaf spot, is a foliar fungal disease of grapes caused by Pseudocercospora vitis (formerly Isariopsis clavispora). It primarily affects leaves late in the season and can cause early defoliation, weakening the vine and reducing yield the following year.
symptoms: Irregular, dark brown to black spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots may coalesce forming large necrotic areas
Grayish-white to dirty-white sporulation visible on underside of lesions
Severely infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely
Lesions may also appear on petioles and young stems
causes: Fungus Pseudocercospora vitis (Isariopsis clavispora)
Favored by warm, humid weather conditions
Spores spread by wind and rain splash
Fungus survives in infected plant debris
treatments: Apply copper-based fungicides or mancozeb at first sign of symptoms
Remove and destroy infected leaves and debris
Apply foliar fungicide programs used for other grape diseases (downy mildew, black rot) may provide control
prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaf debris at end of season
Maintain good vineyard sanitation
Improve air circulation through proper canopy management and pruning
Apply preventive fungicide sprays during warm, humid conditions

description: The grapevine appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage.

Absence of trunk diseases, foliar pathogens, or pest pressure
Consistent moderate irrigation or rainfall without waterlogging
Healthy pruning practices protecting wounds from infection
treatments: Prune vines annually to maintain balanced crop load and open canopy
Apply preventive fungicide program for downy mildew, powdery mildew, and black rot
Protect all pruning wounds with wound sealant or Trichoderma-based products
Monitor for trunk disease symptoms annually after dormant pruning
Apply foliar nutrition (potassium, magnesium, zinc) based on petiole analysis
prevention: Prune vines annually to maintain open canopy and good air circulation
Protect pruning wounds from fungal infections
Practice good sanitation by removing debris and mummified fruit

Apply preventive fungicide programs appropriate to local disease pressure

name: Huanglongbing (Citrus Greening)
description: Huanglongbing (HLB), also known as citrus greening or yellow dragon disease, is the most devastating citrus disease in the world. It is caused by the phloem-restricted bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted primarily by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri). There is currently no cure, and infected trees typically decline and die within a few years.
symptoms: Asymmetrical blotchy mottling and yellowing of leaves (unlike symmetrical nutrient deficiency)
Small, stiff leaves with yellowing along margins and interveinal regions
Twig dieback and progressive decline of the tree
Fruit is small, lopsided, poorly colored, and retains green color at navel end when mature
Fruit has aborted seeds and bitter, sour taste
Premature fruit drop
Overall tree decline and death within a few years
causes: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (most prevalent worldwide form)
Transmitted primarily by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri)
Can also spread through infected grafting material and planting material
Bacteria are phloem-restricted, causing blockage of vascular tissue
treatments: No effective cure currently exists for HLB
Oxytetracycline trunk injection can reduce bacterial titers and temporarily lessen symptoms
Remove and destroy infected trees to reduce inoculum source
Control psyllid populations with insecticides to slow disease spread
Thermotherapy (solar thermotherapy) has shown some promise in research
prevention: Plant only certified HLB-free nursery stock
Control Asian citrus psyllid populations aggressively with insecticides
Implement quarantine measures to prevent movement of infected plant material
Monitor orchards regularly for psyllid activity and disease symptoms
Remove and destroy infected trees immediately upon detection
Avoid introducing plant material from HLB-affected areas

name: Peach Bacterial Spot
description: Bacterial spot is one of the most common and destructive diseases of peach and other stone fruits (Prunus species). It is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni and thrives in areas with hot summers and frequent rainfall. The disease can cause severe defoliation and disfigure fruit, leading to significant economic losses.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that darken to purple-brown with light brown centers
Spots may have a yellow halo; multiple spots cause leaves to turn yellow and drop
Lesions on fruit appear as small, dark, sunken spots
Fruit spots enlarge and crack, creating entry points for other pathogens
Infected branches may develop dark, water-soaked cankers
Severe defoliation in repeated infections weakens trees
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni (also reported as Xanthomonas campestris pv. pruni)
Bacteria overwinter in infected bark and cankers
Spread by rain, wind, and splashing water
Hot, humid conditions with frequent rainfall favor infection
Bacteria enter through stomata, leaf scars, and wounds
treatments: Apply copper-based bactericides preventively starting at bud swell
Continue applications through the season during wet periods
Prune and remove infected branches to reduce bacterial inoculum
Oxytetracycline (Mycoshield) can be effective as a foliar spray
prevention: Plant resistant peach varieties
Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness
Prune trees for good air circulation
Apply preventive copper sprays before infection periods
Practice good orchard sanitation by removing infected debris

name: Healthy
description: The peach plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage.
symptoms: Leaves are bright green, lance-shaped, and free of spots or curl
Fruit develops full size with normal blush, aroma, and firmness
Branches and trunk are smooth and free of cankers or gummosis
Vigorous shoot growth of 12-18 inches annually
Flower buds develop normally and fruit set is adequate
No premature leaf or fruit drop
causes: Well-drained loamy soil with pH 6.0-6.5
Full sun exposure (8+ hours daily)
Balanced nutrition, especially adequate potassium and boron
Consistent irrigation during fruit development without waterlogging
Absence of bacterial spot, brown rot, or peach leaf curl pressure
Proper chilling hours met during winter dormancy
treatments: Apply dormant-season copper spray before bud swell to prevent leaf curl and bacterial spot
Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart for better size and quality
Apply balanced fertilizer based on shoot growth monitoring (12-18 inches annually is ideal)
Monitor for brown rot during warm, wet weather near harvest
Prune annually to maintain an open vase shape for light penetration and air circulation
prevention: Prune annually to improve air circulation
Apply preventive fungicide and bactericide programs
Avoid overhead irrigation
Monitor regularly for early signs of disease or pests
Maintain proper nutrition and soil health

name: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot
description: Bacterial leaf spot is the most common and destructive disease of peppers in the eastern United States. It is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria and thrives in areas with hot summers and frequent rainfall. The disease can devastate pepper crops through early defoliation and fruit disfigurement. There is no cure once established.
symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves starting on lower leaves
Lesions develop into dark purple-brown spots with light brown centers
Spots may have yellow halos
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and drop early
Raised, scab-like cracks and spots on fruit
Stem cankers may also develop
Severe defoliation and in extreme cases plant death
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria (Xanthomonas euvesicatoria)
Bacteria survive in infected seeds and plant debris in soil
Spread by rain splash, overhead irrigation, and handling infected plants
Hot temperatures and frequent rainfall create ideal conditions
Different bacterial races/strains are cultivar-specific
treatments: Apply copper-based bactericides at first sign of disease
Products can suppress spread if applied before disease affects more than 5% of plants
No effective chemical cure once disease is widespread
Remove and destroy heavily infected plant material
prevention: Use disease-free certified seed
Do not plant peppers or tomatoes in the same area for 4-5 years (crop rotation)
Remove all crop debris at end of season and destroy
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at soil level
Do not work in field when plants are wet
Plant resistant pepper varieties when available

name: Healthy
description: The bell pepper plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage.
symptoms: Leaves are dark green, glossy, and free of spots or distortion
Fruit develops firm, thick-walled, with uniform color at maturity
Stems are sturdy and upright
Flowers bloom normally and fruit set is consistent
No wilting, yellowing, or premature fruit drop
Root system is white and healthy
causes: Well-drained, fertile soil with pH 6.0-6.8
Adequate calcium, phosphorus, and potassium availability
Consistent moisture (avoid both drought and waterlogging)
Warm temperatures (70-85°F) for optimal growth
Absence of bacterial spot, Phytophthora, or viral pressure
Proper plant spacing allowing good air circulation
treatments: Apply balanced fertilizer at planting and side-dress with nitrogen at first fruit set
Maintain consistent soil moisture to prevent blossom end rot
Monitor for early signs of bacterial spot, aphids, and thrips
Apply calcium foliar sprays if blossom end rot risk is high
Stake plants if fruit load is heavy to prevent breakage
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed
Practice crop rotation
Water at soil level to avoid wetting foliage
Maintain proper plant spacing for air circulation
Monitor regularly for early signs of disease

name: Potato Early Blight
description: Early blight is a common and widespread fungal disease of potatoes and tomatoes caused primarily by Alternaria linariae (syn. A. tomatophila). It is primarily a leaf spot and foliage blight that typically appears after fruit set. The disease can cause significant defoliation and reduce tuber quality.
symptoms: Circular to irregular dark brown spots on older, lower leaves
Spots form concentric rings creating a target-board or bull's-eye pattern
Yellow area often surrounds the lesions
Multiple lesions coalesce and cause extensive leaf death
Lower leaves affected first, progressing up the plant
In severe cases, complete defoliation of lower leaves
Dark, sunken lesions may also appear on stems and tubers
causes: Fungus Alternaria linariae (formerly A. solani, A. tomatophila)
Spores survive in infected plant debris in soil
Spreads by wind and rain splashing infected soil onto lower leaves
Warm temperatures and wet, humid conditions favor infection
Plants under stress (drought, nutrient deficiency) are more susceptible
treatments: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin) at first sign of symptoms
Remove and destroy infected leaves and plant debris
Apply fungicides preventively in high-risk conditions
prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation to prevent soil splash
Space plants adequately for good air circulation
Practice crop rotation (avoid planting potatoes/tomatoes in the same area)
Remove and destroy all infected crop debris at season end
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash
Stake plants to keep them off the ground

name: Potato Late Blight
description: Late blight is one of the most destructive diseases of potato and tomato, caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans ('plant destroyer'). It was responsible for the Irish potato famine of the 1840s. The disease can spread extremely rapidly under cool, wet conditions and destroy entire crops within weeks.
symptoms: Pale-green to brown, water-soaked spots on leaves that expand rapidly
Lesions turn dark brown and leaves collapse, shrivel, and turn brown
White fuzzy fungal growth (sporangiophores) on underside of leaves in humid conditions
Brown to purple discoloration patches on potato tuber skin
Red-brown rot beneath tuber skin that progresses inward
Brown/black irregular lesions on stems with greasy appearance
Affected tubers may rot in storage
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Survives in infected tubers in soil or storage

name: Squash Powdery Mildew
description: Powdery mildew is one of the most common fungal diseases of squash and other cucurbits, caused primarily by Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum. Unlike most fungal diseases, it thrives in warm, dry conditions with low humidity and does not require wet leaves to develop. It can significantly reduce yield and fruit quality.
symptoms: White, powdery, circular fungal patches on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Powdery growth may spread to cover entire leaf surface
Infected leaves turn yellow, then brown and die
Defoliation reduces photosynthesis and weakens the plant
Stunted growth in severe cases
White powdery growth may also appear on stems and fruit
causes: Fungi Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum
Spores dispersed by wind to new leaf tissue
Warm temperatures (60-80°F) and dry conditions favor development
High plant density and poor air circulation increase risk
Does not require wet leaf surfaces to infect - unlike most fungal diseases

prevention: Plant resistant squash varieties
Space plants adequately for good air circulation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which promotes succulent susceptible growth
Water at soil level in the morning
Monitor plants regularly and address infections early

name: Strawberry Leaf Scorch
description: Strawberry leaf scorch is a fungal disease caused by Diplocarpon earliana (anamorph: Marssonina fragariae). It is the most common leaf disease in matted-row strawberry systems and causes premature leaf death, weakening plants and reducing yield. Disease severity worsens in multi-year plantings.

Purple, sunken streak-like lesions on petioles
Infected sepals turn brown ('dead caps'), reducing fruit attractiveness
Infected fruit may develop discolored streaks or sunken lesions

Plant in light, well-drained soil with good air circulation
Choose disease-resistant strawberry cultivars

name: Tomato Bacterial Spot
description: Bacterial spot is one of the most common bacterial diseases of tomatoes, caused by Xanthomonas vesicatoria and related Xanthomonas species. It is particularly problematic in warm, wet growing seasons and can cause significant defoliation and fruit spotting. The bacteria survive on infected seeds and crop debris.
symptoms: Small (1/8 inch or less), dark, water-soaked spots on leaves with yellow halos
Spots enlarge and run together under wet conditions, turning dark brown to black

name: Tomato Early Blight
description: Early blight is one of the most common fungal diseases of tomatoes, caused primarily by Alternaria linariae. Symptoms typically appear after fruit set and begin on older, lower leaves. In severe cases, plants can be almost completely defoliated, significantly reducing yield.

Spores survive in infected plant debris in soil

name: Tomato Late Blight
description: Late blight is one of the most destructive diseases of tomatoes, caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It spreads very rapidly under cool, wet conditions and can kill entire plants and crops within a short period. It is the same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine.

Avoid overhead irrigation

name: Tomato Leaf Mold
description: Tomato leaf mold is a fungal disease caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum). It is primarily a disease of greenhouse and high-tunnel tomatoes where humidity is high, but also occurs in field tomatoes. The disease causes velvety spore masses on the underside of leaves, leading to defoliation and reduced yield.
symptoms: Pale green or yellowish spots on the upper surface of leaves
Velvety, olive-green to grayish-brown spore masses (mold) on underside of leaves
Infected leaves curl, wither, and drop prematurely
Severe infections can cause complete defoliation
Reduced fruit set and yield
Rarely affects fruit directly, but blossom end infections are possible

High relative humidity (>85%) strongly favors disease development
Spores are airborne and spread easily within enclosed growing environments
Fungus survives on crop debris and greenhouse surfaces
Warm temperatures (72-75°F) combined with high humidity are optimal for infection

Remove and destroy infected leaves
Increase ventilation and reduce humidity in greenhouses

Avoid overhead irrigation and water in the morning

Remove and destroy infected plant debris at end of season

Stake and prune plants to improve air circulation

name: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot
description: Septoria leaf spot is one of the two most common fungal diseases of tomatoes (along with early blight), caused by Septoria lycopersici. It is primarily a leaf disease that begins at the base of plants and moves upward. Rapid defoliation in severe cases significantly reduces yield and fruit quality.

name: Tomato Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite)
description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are tiny arachnids that feed on the underside of tomato leaves by piercing plant cells and removing their contents. They are not a fungal or bacterial disease but a pest infestation. They thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions and can quickly build large populations causing significant damage.

name: Tomato Target Spot
description: Tomato target spot is a fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola. It can affect leaves, stems, and fruit, and is particularly common in warm, humid tropical and subtropical regions. The disease gets its name from the target-like concentric ring lesions it produces. It can cause significant defoliation and fruit loss.

name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
description: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is one of the most serious viral diseases affecting tomato plants, especially in tropical and subtropical areas. It is a DNA virus from the family Geminiviridae transmitted exclusively by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. It can cause yield losses of 90-100% when infection occurs during early growth stages.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of young leaves at the top of the plant
Yellowing of leaf margins and interveinal areas
Reduced leaflet size
Severe plant stunting - plants become bushy with shortened internodes
Erect, upright shoot growth
Flower drop and poor fruit set
Infected young plants rarely produce marketable fruit

Warm climates and high whitefly populations increase disease incidence

Apply systemic insecticides (imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) to control whitefly vector
Remove and destroy infected plants to reduce virus source
Yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce whitefly populations
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato varieties
Use reflective mulches to repel whiteflies
Cover young transplants with fine-mesh insect netting to exclude whiteflies
Apply systemic insecticides at transplanting and throughout season
Remove infected plants immediately to prevent virus spread
Control weed hosts of whitefly near tomato fields
Monitor regularly for whitefly populations

name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV)
description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a highly stable RNA virus closely related to Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) that can severely affect tomato plants. Unlike TYLCV, it is spread primarily through mechanical contact - contaminated hands, tools, and plant-to-plant contact rather than insect vectors. It can survive for years in dried infected plant material.
symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green areas on leaves
Leaf distortion, curling, and malformation
Stunted plant growth
Young leaves curl upward and are reduced in size
Mottled, streaked, or distorted fruit
Uneven fruit ripening
Necrotic streaking on stems and leaves in some strains
causes: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV), a tobamovirus (RNA virus)
Spread mechanically through contaminated hands, tools, and clothing
Can persist for years in dried infected plant material and seed coats
Spreads rapidly from plant to plant during handling (pruning, transplanting)
Infected seed can carry the virus
Tobacco products can also serve as a contamination source (related TMV)

Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Sanitize tools with 1:10 bleach solution between plants
Wash hands thoroughly after handling infected plants
prevention: Plant ToMV-resistant tomato varieties (varieties with Tm-1, Tm-2, or Tm-2² resistance genes)
Use certified virus-free seed
Treat seed with hot water before planting
Wash hands thoroughly before handling plants, especially after using tobacco products
Disinfect tools with bleach or 70% alcohol between plants
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Do not use tobacco products when working with tomatoes
